title: Nobody feels qualified
text: Many successful professionals, {{1}} colleagues regard as plainly competent, privately suspect they have been promoted by mistake. {{2}} feeling was named the imposter syndrome in 1978, when psychologists Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes noticed how common such doubts were {{3}} high-achieving women; later research found the pattern across genders and professions. Sufferers discount praise, put their successes {{4}} to luck or timing, and live with the dread of being found out. Cruelly, {{5}} more a person achieves, the stronger the feeling often becomes, because each new role raises the stakes. Naming the pattern helps, precisely {{6}} imposter feelings thrive on the false belief that everyone else is certain, and discovering that respected colleagues share the doubt turns {{7}} was a shameful secret into a shared, survivable quirk of ambitious minds. Mentors are now advised to raise it openly {{8}} new joiners, since the first months of a new job are when the doubt bites hardest.

gaps.explanation: Object relative after the comma about people: whom.
The feeling is defined by what follows: the definite article.

gaps.hint: particle: put their successes ___ to luck
gaps.explanation: 'Put down to' — the particle completes the phrasal verb.

gaps.hint: article: ___ more a person achieves, the stronger
gaps.explanation: 'The more…, the stronger…' — the double comparative.

gaps.hint: conjunction: helps, precisely ___ imposter feelings thrive
pronoun: turns ___ was a shameful secret
gaps.explanation: 'Turns what was X into Y' — the fused relative as object.

gaps.hint: preposition: raise it openly ___ new joiners
gaps.explanation: 'Raise something with someone' — the person takes 'with'.
